misconceptions.statement: Plastic is made from natural things like trees and plants, so it is a natural material.
misconceptions.why: Plastic feels like wood or paper and students link all materials to nature.
misconceptions.fix: Most plastics are made in factories from petroleum and natural gas, which are fossil fuels. Only a few bioplastics use plant material.

probe.question: What is most ordinary plastic made from?

misconceptions.root_belief: all materials come directly from nature

misconceptions.statement: Plastic is a single substance, like one metal.
misconceptions.why: The word plastic is used as one name for many things.
misconceptions.fix: Plastic is a name for many different polymers such as PET, HDPE and PVC, each with different properties.

probe.question: Are all plastics the same material?

misconceptions.root_belief: one common name means one single thing

misconceptions.statement: Plastic does not rot because it is a dead material, not alive like leaves.
misconceptions.why: Students link rotting with things that were once alive.
misconceptions.fix: Plastic does not rot because microbes lack the enzymes to digest its strong long chain molecules, so it is non-biodegradable.

probe.question: Why does a plastic bottle not rot in soil?

misconceptions.root_belief: only living things change or decay

misconceptions.statement: Plastic does not rot because it is waterproof, so water cannot reach it.
misconceptions.why: Students notice plastic repels water and assume water is needed for rot.
misconceptions.fix: Plastic resists decay because bacteria and fungi cannot break its chemical bonds. Being waterproof is not the main reason.

probe.question: Why does plastic stay for years in wet soil?

misconceptions.root_belief: one visible property explains everything

misconceptions.statement: When plastic breaks into tiny pieces, it has disappeared from the environment.
misconceptions.why: What you cannot see seems gone.
misconceptions.fix: Breaking into small pieces only makes microplastics. The plastic is still there and can last for centuries.

probe.question: A plastic bag crumbles into tiny bits in sunlight. Is the plastic gone?

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student ideas on decay and disappearance of matter

misconceptions.statement: Plastic takes only a few years to disappear in nature, like paper.
misconceptions.why: Students compare plastic with paper and fruit peel without knowing real timescales.
misconceptions.fix: A plastic bottle may take hundreds of years to break down, and some plastics are never fully removed in a human lifetime.

probe.question: About how long does a plastic bottle last in the environment?

misconceptions.root_belief: all waste vanishes in similar short time

misconceptions.statement: Single-use plastic means plastic that can only be used once because it breaks after one use.
misconceptions.why: The name is read literally as a physical limit.
misconceptions.fix: Single-use plastics are designed to be thrown away after one use, but they are strong enough to be used many times and last for centuries as waste.

probe.question: Why is a plastic carry bag called single-use?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Anything labelled biodegradable plastic will rot quickly in a dustbin or in the sea.
misconceptions.why: The label sounds like a guarantee of quick decay anywhere.
misconceptions.fix: Many biodegradable plastics need industrial composting heat and conditions, and may stay for a long time in soil or the sea.

probe.question: A biodegradable plastic bag is thrown in a river. What happens?

misconceptions.root_belief: a label guarantees the property everywhere

misconceptions.statement: Microplastics are tiny living organisms that grow in plastic.
misconceptions.why: The prefix micro is linked with microbes and microscopic life.
misconceptions.fix: Microplastics are non-living plastic pieces smaller than 5 mm. They are not organisms.

probe.question: What are microplastics?
probe.wrong_answer: Tiny living organisms found on plastic

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Microplastics are too small to matter or harm anything.
misconceptions.why: Small size is taken to mean small effect.
misconceptions.fix: Microplastics are eaten by small animals, move up food chains and have been found in fish, salt, water and human bodies. Their effects are still being studied.

probe.question: Are microplastics a bigger or smaller problem than a plastic bag?

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' ideas about scale and size in environmental science

misconceptions.statement: Microplastics come only from big plastic items breaking up.
misconceptions.why: Students think only of fragmentation of visible litter.
misconceptions.fix: Microplastics also come from microbeads in some cosmetics, from synthetic clothes shedding fibres in washing, and from tyre wear.

probe.question: Name the only source of microplastics.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: Only sea animals are harmed by plastic; land animals like cows are not.
misconceptions.why: Media images focus on turtles and whales.
misconceptions.fix: Cows, goats and birds on land also eat plastic bags from garbage, which can block their stomachs and kill them.

probe.question: Can a cow be harmed by plastic?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only sea animals are harmed

misconceptions.root_belief: a problem exists only where it is shown

misconceptions.statement: Ocean plastic comes mostly from ships and fishermen, not from our towns.
misconceptions.why: The ocean seems far from city life.
misconceptions.fix: A large share of ocean plastic is land litter carried by drains, rivers and wind. Fishing gear is one important part, but not the main source.

probe.question: Where does most ocean plastic come from?

misconceptions.root_belief: problems are caused by someone far away

misconceptions.statement: The triangle recycling symbol on a plastic item means it can be recycled everywhere.
misconceptions.why: The arrow triangle looks like a general recycling sign.
misconceptions.fix: The number inside the triangle shows the type of plastic. Whether it is actually recycled depends on local facilities, and some types like 3, 6 and 7 are rarely recycled.

probe.question: A cup shows a triangle with number 6. What does that tell you?

misconceptions.root_belief: a symbol means what it looks like

misconceptions.statement: Plastic can be recycled forever, again and again, with no loss of quality.
misconceptions.why: Recycling is shown as a perfect loop.
misconceptions.fix: Plastics lose quality each time they are recycled, so most can be recycled only a few times before becoming waste.

probe.question: How many times can a plastic bottle be recycled?

misconceptions.root_belief: a cycle diagram means perfect endless repeat

misconceptions.statement: Dirty mixed plastic can be thrown together into a recycling bin and recycled.
misconceptions.why: Students think the recycling plant sorts and cleans everything.
misconceptions.fix: Food-soiled and mixed plastics spoil a batch, so plastics should be rinsed and separated by type for good recycling.

probe.question: Should a greasy plastic wrapper go with clean bottles for recycling?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all plastic can go together

misconceptions.root_belief: the machine will fix any mistake

misconceptions.statement: Burning plastic gets rid of it completely, leaving nothing behind.
misconceptions.why: Fire seems to make things vanish into ash or smoke.
misconceptions.fix: Burning turns plastic into toxic gases like dioxins and carbon monoxide and ash that harm health and air. The atoms are not destroyed.

probe.question: What happens to plastic when it is burnt in the open?
probe.wrong_answer: It disappears and the problem is solved

misconceptions.root_belief: burning destroys matter completely
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' ideas of combustion and conservation of matter

misconceptions.statement: Burning plastic is harmless because the smoke is just like smoke from wood.
misconceptions.why: All smoke looks similar.
misconceptions.fix: Burning plastic, especially PVC, releases poisonous gases such as dioxins that can cause breathing problems and cancer. Wood smoke is different in what it contains.

probe.question: Is it safe to burn plastic waste near houses?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is just smoke like from wood

misconceptions.root_belief: things that look alike behave alike

misconceptions.statement: Burying plastic in the ground solves the plastic problem because it is hidden.
misconceptions.why: Out of sight is treated as out of the way.
misconceptions.fix: Buried plastic stays for hundreds of years and may leak chemicals into soil and groundwater. Burying only stores it.

probe.question: Is burying plastic a permanent solution?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, once buried it is gone

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: If plastic can be recycled, it is fine to use as much as we like.
misconceptions.why: Recycling is seen as cancelling the harm of use.
misconceptions.fix: Recycling is the last of the three Rs. Reducing and reusing save more resources, and much plastic is never actually recycled.

probe.question: Which is better for the environment: recycling many bottles or using fewer bottles?
probe.wrong_answer: Recycling many, as it is all the same

misconceptions.root_belief: one fix cancels the whole problem

misconceptions.statement: Plastic litter on the road is only an ugly sight and does not affect anything else.
misconceptions.why: Litter is seen as a looks problem.
misconceptions.fix: Plastic blocks drains and can cause waterlogging and floods, and can breed mosquitoes in stagnant water.

probe.question: How can plastic in drains cause trouble in the monsoon?
probe.wrong_answer: It cannot, it only looks dirty

misconceptions.root_belief: a problem has only one kind of effect
